Dermatology · published research

Scleroderma

Small studies report improved perfusion, ulcer healing, or local symptoms in selected scleroderma manifestations. They do not establish an effect on systemic fibrosis or internal-organ disease.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Small studies report improved perfusion, ulcer healing, or local symptoms in selected scleroderma manifestations. They do not establish an effect on systemic fibrosis or internal-organ disease.

Summary of the Evidence

Seven publications are relevant when four exact-category reports are combined with three narrowly mapped systemic-sclerosis studies on digital or skin ulcers and xerostomia. The exact group includes two case reports, a ten-person cutaneous-sclerosis series, and a seven-person infrared-A hyperthermia series. The mapped reports include one case report and small cohorts of eight and twelve. These publications address different local problems and are not seven independent tests of systemic disease modification.

Human and clinical evidence

A feasibility study treated 14 digital ulcers in eight people with systemic sclerosis using a custom LED device. Patient and clinician ulcer ratings improved during follow-up, and laser-Doppler perfusion increased immediately after exposure. The study reported no safety concerns, but it was small and designed primarily to assess feasibility and tolerability (Hughes et al. 2019).

A separate retrospective study of scleroderma skin ulcers reported complete healing in 5 of 12 treated cases during blue-light treatment. Participants also received systemic treatment, wound-bed preparation, and local care, so the contribution of light cannot be isolated (Spinella et al. 2022). A ten-person cutaneous-sclerosis series reported sustained improvement in seven participants, while a CREST case report described local functional and symptom changes. A small xerostomia case and a thermal infrared-A series report local outcomes, including fewer Raynaud attacks, but they use different endpoints and are not equivalent to nonthermal PBM for skin fibrosis.

Animal evidence

No animal study directly relevant to scleroderma was identified in these categories.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No scleroderma-specific cell or ex-vivo study was identified in the reviewed records.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The digital-ulcer feasibility study used 405-nm violet visible, 660-nm red visible, and 850-nm near-infrared LEDs at 10 J/cm², twice weekly for three weeks. The blue-light ulcer cohort used a different device and wound-care protocol. A separate infrared-A hyperthermia series intentionally warmed tissue and should not be grouped as nonthermal PBM. These different approaches have not been compared head to head.

Interpretation

The available findings concern local ulcers, skin changes, or symptoms, and some patients improved on those measures. They do not show that PBM changes systemic sclerosis, internal-organ involvement, or the underlying course of fibrosis. The most defensible interpretation is a preliminary local-treatment signal that needs controlled, manifestation-specific testing.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for selected local skin or digital-ulcer outcomes Very low for systemic disease modification
Publications and records7 articles (3 narrowly mapped systemic-sclerosis reports)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Small local studies report improved ulcer perfusion, healing, symptoms, or skin appearance, but they examine different manifestations and mostly lack randomized controls. One digital-ulcer feasibility study used light alongside usual care, and another ulcer cohort was retrospective. Larger controlled studies of the same manifestation with standard care kept consistent would be needed to judge reproducibility and systemic effects.
